source: Shin, Polyanskaya, Lucero, Oulasvirta (2025) No Evidence for LLMs Being Useful in Problem Reframing
finding: Largest test of LLMs in Dorst-style problem reframing. LLM help did not raise the novelty or usefulness of designers' frames compared with working alone.
numbers: 456 crowd designers recruited, 280 kept after filters (145 women, 128 men, 7 other). 4 arms: manual, direct (LLM-made frames only), structured (Dorst 9-step with GPT-4o at each step), free-form chat. 3 hard design problems. 15 high-expertise raters scored novelty and usefulness. Power analysis: 220 and 280 needed for 95% power at medium effect; no significant difference for manual vs all-LLM on either measure.
quote: using LLMs in problem reframing does not aid designers in generating more novel or useful problem frames
limits: Crowd designers, one session (about 21-28 min), one model (GPT-4o, Aug 2024), no reasoning model. A null result at medium-effect power; small effects not excluded. Participants picked their own best frame.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that bolting a plain LLM onto reframing gives no measured gain. Matches our schema note that O8 is [S] and LLM reframing is null in one large test.

source: Shin, Polyanskaya, Lucero, Oulasvirta (2025) No Evidence for LLMs Being Useful in Problem Reframing (process and time)
finding: The structured arm was the Dorst nine-step process turned into button-driven GPT-4o prompts. It took longest and users regenerated a lot, yet quality did not improve.
numbers: Mean time per two frames: manual 23.25 min (SD 14.73), direct 21.82 (11.95), structured 28.35 (18.00), free-form 20.78 (9.34). In the structured arm all participants but one regenerated all content at least once; most regenerated item was the apparent problem (n=39), then stakeholder view (n=25).
limits: Standardized prompts so prompting skill did not vary. This also means free skilled prompting is untested beyond the free-form arm.
agent_relevance: Wrapping the nine Dorst steps around a model is not enough by itself. Cost went up (time, regenerations) with no quality return.

source: Shin, Polyanskaya, Lucero, Oulasvirta (2025) No Evidence for LLMs Being Useful in Problem Reframing (perceived help)
finding: People felt the LLM helped, but the three ways of using it did not differ in felt help, effort, agency or ownership. Felt help is not evidence of better frames.
numbers: Creativity Support Index: direct 64.28 (SD 18.90), structured 64.85 (20.00), free-form 61.01 (17.19); all in the good-support band (50-90). No significant differences between approaches in CSI or NASA-TLX. 34% of post-survey respondents said LLM frames were not novel enough to build on.
limits: Self-report. Authors link flat NASA-TLX to the irony of automation.
agent_relevance: Do not use the model's or the user's sense of usefulness as the signal for a good reframe. Use a check (G2, G3).

source: Shin, Polyanskaya, Lucero, Oulasvirta (2025) No Evidence for LLMs Being Useful in Problem Reframing (expertise gap)
finding: With LLMs, people who understood reframing well made more novel frames than people who did not. LLMs widened the gap instead of closing it.
numbers: Experts = 3 or more of 5 quiz items correct. Expert vs novice novelty with LLM: 12.54% higher for experts (t=2.70, p=0.01); free-form gap 20.84% (p=0.06, not significant). Experts felt more agency (t=2.05, p=0.04); structured arm 15.69% more (t=2.29, p=0.02). No usefulness gap. Expert/novice split balanced across arms (chi2(3, N=280)=0.70, p=0.87).
limits: Post-hoc split by quiz; no no-LLM expert baseline reported in this contrast.
agent_relevance: The gain from a reframe tool depends on a skilled controller. For our agent, the program (not the model) must supply the frame-selection judgement.

source: Sood, Wan, Paris, Grace (2026) What makes LLM-generated Answers Valuable for Research Problem Reframing? (ICCC 2026)
finding: Small study where a prompt built on Dorst's frame steps beat plain question answering and plain context stuffing at producing answers researchers found interesting.
numbers: 7 research students, 3 questions each, 27 answers each (3 per strategy per question, 189 answers per strategy overall). First-pass interesting: dorst-frame 29/189, direct 17/189, all-content 17/189. Top-3 rankings (21 slots): dorst-frame 11 (52%), direct 7 (33%), all-content 3 (14%). 6 of 7 participants rated dorst-frame answers interesting most often. Model: gpt-oss-120b.
limits: n=7, no statistics, one model, interesting is not reframed. Only steps 1-3 and 6 of Dorst's nine were used. Authors say whether people actually reframed is unknown.
agent_relevance: The one positive result for a Dorst-structured prompt. Same context given as plain input did worse, so structure of processing mattered, not only information. Weak evidence; test before using.

source: Sood et al. (2026) (answer profiles)
finding: Useful answers fell in two kinds: reinforcing (clear up my thinking, I am on track) and reorienting (taught me something new, challenged my view, connected to something new). Only the reorienting kind carries reframing potential.
numbers: 7-point Likert Q1-Q7 on 21 top-3 answers. Q1, Q3, Q4 cluster (reorienting); Q2, Q5 cluster (reinforcing). Surprise (Q6) tracks challenge (Q3) and feeling off track (Q5). 5 of 7 said top-3 answers made them rethink their question to some extent.
limits: Clusters from 21 ratings. Surprise meant different things to different people.
agent_relevance: Gives a cheap test for a candidate reframe: does it change which facts matter (reorienting) or just restate the current plan (reinforcing)? Could be a code-checkable label.

source: Sood et al. (2026) (failure modes)
finding: Useless LLM answers had named faults: misread terms, assumed knowledge the user lacked, numbers with no justification, forced links between unrelated papers, did not answer the question.
numbers: Quoted participant remarks (P1, P2, P3, P4, P5, P7). With theory-heavy notes the model forced connections between all papers.
limits: Qualitative, 7 people.
agent_relevance: Failure list for a reframe filter: reject a reframe that uses unstated assumptions or ignores the stated goal.

source: Zheng, Mishra, Chen, Cheng, Chi, Le, Zhou (2024) Take a Step Back: Evoking Reasoning via Abstraction in LLMs (ICLR 2024)
finding: Ask the model first for the high-level principle or concept behind the question, then answer using it. This is a machine version of moving up one level of frame. Large gains on physics, chemistry and time-based QA.
numbers: PaLM-2L: MMLU Physics 66.4 -> 73.2, Chemistry 70.9 -> 81.8 (CoT 65.0 and 75.3). GPT-4: Physics 69.4 -> 84.5 (CoT 82.9), Chemistry 80.9 -> 85.6 (CoT 85.3). Llama2-70B: 51.9 -> 64.8 and 55.7 -> 66.7. TimeQA PaLM-2L 41.5 -> 66.0 (RAG 57.4; step-back plus RAG 68.7; GPT-4 63.2). MuSiQue +7 points for PaLM-2L; best GPT-4 numbers 42.8 (MuSiQue) and 86.4 (StrategyQA).
quote: improves PaLM-2L performance on MMLU (Physics and Chemistry) by 7% and 11% respectively, TimeQA by 27%
limits: Few-shot abstraction exemplars were written by hand per task. Gain over CoT is small for GPT-4 on chemistry (+0.3). Mostly benchmark QA, not open design problems.
agent_relevance: Closest tested method to O8 reframe-the-goal as a step-back. Cheap, one extra call. Note it abstracts always, not on a failure signal, so G1 would gate it.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) Step-Back (error analysis)
finding: Abstraction rarely fails. The remaining errors come from the later reasoning step, so a better frame does not fix weak reasoning.
numbers: On MMLU high-school Physics, Step-Back fixes 20.5% of baseline errors and introduces 11.9% new ones. Of Step-Back's own errors, more than 90% occur in the Reasoning step; Principle Error (abstraction step) is a small share; Reasoning Error and Math Error are the largest classes.
limits: Error classes hand-annotated on PaLM-2L. Net gain is positive but 11.9% new errors means a frame can also hurt.
agent_relevance: A reframe can break items that were right. Needs a held-out check (G3) before adopting the new frame. Pair with code verification of the later steps.

source: Deng, Zhang, Chen, Gu (2024) Rephrase and Respond: Let LLMs Ask Better Questions for Themselves
finding: Letting the model rewrite the user's question before answering raises accuracy on tasks where the question is ambiguous. A weaker form of reframing: restating, not changing the goal.
numbers: GPT-4 zero-shot, 10 tasks. Average accuracy: original questions 64.95, main RaR prompt about 89.8, other RaR wordings 87.2-89.0. Examples (original -> RaR): Day 54.29 -> 93.33, Year 57.14 -> 89.52, Last-letter-4 21.36 -> 86.82, Coin flip 74.55 -> 99.09; CSQA 84.09 -> 85.45 (little room). Sports: GPT-3.5 and Vicuna sometimes got slightly worse.
limits: Task set partly built for ambiguity. Gains largest for GPT-4, modest for Vicuna-13B. Table was parsed from a PDF layout; pairing of baseline and RaR rows is by position.
agent_relevance: Restating the problem is cheap and helps when the wording is the issue. It is not a change of frame; keep it separate from O8.

source: Deng et al. (2024) RaR (two-step and few-shot CoT)
finding: A stronger model's rephrasing can be passed to a weaker responder (two-step RaR). RaR also stacks on few-shot CoT.
numbers: Last-letter task GPT-4 (2 and 4 letters): one-shot CoT 89.04 / 78.18 vs RaR+one-shot CoT 100 / 93.64 (as parsed); four-shot CoT 87.21 / 52.27 vs RaR+four-shot 100 / 95.45. Zero-shot CoT on Chinese Idiom: 31.43%, worse than the original question.
limits: Layout-parsed table. Zero-shot CoT hurt on the hard idiom task, showing that adding reasoning can fail where restating helps.
agent_relevance: A rewrite of the problem can fix errors that more reasoning does not. A model can reframe for another model.

source: Mishra, Khashabi, Baral, Choi, Hajishirzi (2022) Reframing Instructional Prompts to GPTk's Language (ACL Findings)
finding: Human-written reframings of task instructions (shorter, itemized, decomposed, restrained, specialized) gave large few-shot gains on older GPT models.
numbers: 12 NLP tasks, 6 categories (Natural Instructions). Reframed prompts raised few-shot performance of GPT3-series by 12.5% and GPT2-series by 6.7% on average. Five reframing types: pattern, itemizing, decomposition, restraining, specialization. On answer-generation and incorrect-answer-generation, GPT3 few-shot with reframing beat supervised baselines by 11% and 4% absolute.
limits: Reframing done by hand by the authors; old models (GPT-3 era). Best technique differs by task type; decomposition helps fewer task types. Reframed instructions were shorter than the originals.
agent_relevance: Early evidence that how a task is worded matters as much as raw model skill. Modern models may need this less; test.

source: Mishra et al. (2022) (error analysis)
finding: Reframing fixes many errors but also causes some, and keeps many.
numbers: Error analysis: reframing corrects 24% of the raw-instruction mistakes while causing 4% additional failures; 31% of errors are failures of the raw instruction that reframing retains. Task-level decomposition lets an early error pass down to later steps.
limits: Qualitative analysis on a sample.
agent_relevance: Decomposed reframes can propagate a first-step error. Verify each step with code.

source: Li et al. (2025) Solving Situation Puzzles with Large Language Model and External Reformulation
finding: On lateral-thinking (situation) puzzles, ChatGPT gets stuck in long dialogs asking over-detailed or repeated questions. Restarting with a rewritten puzzle that includes the confirmed Q&A helped.
numbers: 5 puzzles; max 30 questions and 5 guesses. Baseline vs reformulation: wins/losses 2/3 -> 4/1, questions 28.6 -> 22.6, guesses 2.8 -> 2.4, yes-answers 3.6 -> 5, no-answers 18.2 -> 12.2, irrelevant 6.8 -> 5.4. Trigger K=5 rounds, M=3 kept Q&A: 4/1; wrong-guess-only trigger 3/2; K=10,M=6 3/2.
limits: Tiny sample (5 puzzles), one ChatGPT model, no statistics. An arXiv preprint, not peer reviewed.
agent_relevance: A working reframe-on-stall loop: detect a dialog plateau by count, then restart from a compacted statement. Matches G1 (signal-driven) and suggests a count-based trigger is usable.

source: Jiang, Ilievski, Ma, Sourati (2023) BRAINTEASER: Lateral Thinking Puzzles for Large Language Models (EMNLP 2023)
finding: Puzzles that need breaking the default commonsense frame are hard for models. The strongest tested model (ChatGPT) reached about 53% and 63% against about 92% for humans.
numbers: 1,100 puzzles (sentence and word types) plus semantic and context reconstructions; random 25%; human 91.67 on a 102-question sample by 3 experts. ChatGPT about 53 (sentence) and 63 (word) per the text. Many models near random. Instruction-tuned models did better on word puzzles, commonsense models slightly better on sentence puzzles.
limits: Multiple-choice format; ChatGPT may have memorised some word puzzles (it opened with 'the question seems to be a brain teaser' on the COW-in-thirteen-letters item).
agent_relevance: The standard test of frame-breaking in LLMs. It is also the BRAINTEASER benchmark in HTSA. Any O8 variant should be scored here against plain.

source: Jiang et al. (2023) BRAINTEASER (few-shot)
finding: Adding more examples did not reliably help ChatGPT on lateral puzzles; scores moved up and down with shot count.
numbers: ChatGPT zero-shot sentence puzzle 59.17, two-shot 62.20; other cells moved non-monotonically with shots (for example 33.97 at six-shot in one column). Exact column labels were not recovered from the PDF layout.
limits: Table columns were hard to parse; treat individual cells as approximate.
agent_relevance: Examples alone do not install frame-shifting. Supports using a structural step instead of more shots.

source: Zhou, Pujara, Ren, Chen, Cheng, Le, Chi, Zhou, Mishra, Zheng (2024) Self-Discover: LLMs Self-Compose Reasoning Structures
finding: The model selects, adapts and plans which reasoning modules to use for the task before solving. This is task-level framing chosen by the model.
numbers: Accuracy, direct / CoT / Plan-and-Solve / Self-Discover: PaLM 2-L BBH 56 / 60 / 61 / 67, T4D 30 / 40 / 42 / 69, MATH 45 / 42 / 49 / 50.5. GPT-4 BBH 58 / 75 / 73 / 81, T4D 51 / 52 / 53 / 85, MATH 70.5 / 71 / 70 / 73. Up to 32% over CoT; beats CoT-Self-Consistency by more than 20% with 10-40x less inference compute.
limits: Gains are biggest on world-knowledge and agent tasks (T4D) and small on MATH (+1.5 to +3). Structures made by the model itself; most failures were in computation.
agent_relevance: Evidence that a one-time frame step (choose approach, then solve) is worth its cost. Fits as a planned operator, but G1 says do not fire it on a schedule.

source: Echterhoff, Liu, Alessa, McAuley, He (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs
finding: Models show a human-like framing effect: the same admissions case gets different decisions under admit versus reject wording. Debiasing prompts help unevenly.
numbers: Admission rate under admit vs reject framing, baseline: GPT-4 0.375 vs 0.780 (difference -0.405, i.e. 40.5% more admitted in the reject framing). Mitigations shifted this widely: GPT-4 selfhelp 0.270 vs 0.280 (-0.010), GPT-4 counterfactual 0.370 vs 0.940 (-0.570). Few-shot debiasing sometimes drove admission to near 0 or 1 (marked as instruction failure).
limits: Admissions scenario only; 400 prompts per test for GPT. Covered in depth by the preference-construction subfield, listed here only as the link: wording of a frame changes the answer.
agent_relevance: Warning: reframes change decisions even when facts are identical. A reframing step must be tested for such drift. Cross-link to risky-choice framing and framing and preference construction.

source: Qi, Lee, Breazeal, Park (2025) Does Reasoning with Large Language Models Improve Recognizing, Generating and Reframing Unhelpful Thoughts?
finding: On cognitive-reframing tasks, a light task-fit prompt method beat the big reasoning models on recognition, and reasoning models were not better at writing reframes.
numbers: Task 1 (name the unhelpful thought pattern), accuracy: GPT-3.5 0.425, GPT-4 0.504, GPT-4o 0.597, o1 0.560, o3-mini 0.549, DeepSeek-R1-70B 0.527, Llama-3.3 0.558; GPT-3.5+DoT 0.956; +CoT 0.395, +SC 0.419, +ToT 0.434. Reframe generation (Task 3, ROUGE): best GPT-3.5+SC 0.307, GPT-3.5 0.287, o1 0.126. Strategy-aligned reframe (Task 4): GPT-3.5 0.272 and +SC 0.275 strongest; o1 0.134; all scored lower than Task 3.
limits: Clinical cognitive reframing, not design framing. ROUGE and embedding similarity to one reference reframe are weak quality measures.
agent_relevance: Shows more thinking tokens can make reframe writing worse. Argues against forcing long reasoning at the reframe step; use diverse short samples then let code select.

source: Qi et al. (2025) (compute versus result)
finding: More output tokens helped recognition of the thought pattern but hurt reframe generation. Reasoning-trained models cost much more and did not write better reframes.
numbers: Linear fit of output tokens against score: positive slope for recognition (Task 1), negative for reframe generation (Task 3). Task 3 ROUGE: o1 0.126 vs GPT-3.5 0.287.
limits: Single reference-based metric; one dataset (PatternReframe).
agent_relevance: Do not spend a long chain of thought on the reframe slot.

source: Sharma, Rushton, Lin, Wadden, Lucas, Miner, Nguyen, Althoff (2023) Cognitive Reframing of Negative Thoughts through Human-Language Model Interaction (ACL 2023)
finding: Large field test of LM-written reframes. People preferred reframes that were empathic and specific, and did not prefer very positive ones.
numbers: Randomized field study, 2,067 participants on a mental-health site; 7 linguistic attributes defined. Highly empathic reframes preferred 55.7% more often (39.7% vs 25.5%, p<1e-5); highly specific preferred 43.1% more often (39.2% vs 27.4%); highly positive preferred 22.7% less often (29.6% vs 38.3%). Relatable and helpful ratings rose with rationality and specificity (e.g. 3.91 vs 3.53, p<0.05). Authors' model: 11.2% higher BLEU, 9.7% higher ROUGE than baselines.
limits: Self-chosen preference and ratings, not long-term outcome. Clinical, not design; the authors flag generic or wrong-assumption outputs among flagged items.
agent_relevance: Reframe quality can be scored by checkable attributes (specific, actionable, rational), not only taste. Too-positive reframes were disliked: a reframe must not dodge the problem.

source: Dorst (2015) Frame Innovation: Create New Thinking by Design (MIT Press)
finding: Describes frame creation as a nine-step process: archaeology, paradox, context, field, themes, frame, futures, transformation, integration. Both LLM tests above (Shin 2025; Sood 2026) built prompts from this list.
numbers: Step list taken from how Sood 2026 describes it; the book itself was not opened.
limits: Process description from practice and case studies, not a controlled experiment.
agent_relevance: Gives the step names an agent loop could use as slots. Evidence that following them helps is only the weak 2026 study.

source: Schon (1983) The Reflective Practitioner; Dorst and Cross (2001) Creativity in the design process: co-evolution of problem-solution (Design Studies)
finding: Designers move between problem and solution and change the problem frame as they learn from trial solutions. This is the base claim LLM studies cite. Not opened this session.
numbers: As cited by Shin 2025 and Sood 2026 (co-evolution of problem and solution spaces with feedback). No numbers taken here.
limits: Protocol study of a small number of designers; details not checked here.
agent_relevance: Motivates O8 triggering on what a failing output says about the goal (G2), not on opinion.

source: Maher and Poon (1996) design exploration as co-evolution; Gero and Kannengiesser (2014) FBS ontology
finding: Older computational models of reframing: a genetic-algorithm style model of problem-solution co-evolution, and the Function-Behaviour-Structure ontology where the most radical reformulation changes the function space. The FBS claim is as cited in Sood 2026; the Maher and Poon description is from memory.
numbers: Not opened. No numbers recorded.
limits: Verify before use.
agent_relevance: Precedent for treating reframing as a search over problem definitions, not only over solutions.

source: HTSA project note (SCHEMA.md, operator O8 row)
finding: Our schema already lists O8 Reframe the goal with evidence [S] and notes LLM reframing was null in one large test, and G1 says rethink only on a signal.
numbers: O8 fires after naming what the failing output says about the framing. Sources listed: Schon; Dorst and Cross; F06.
limits: Internal document.
agent_relevance: The studies here back keeping O8 gated and checked: Shin 2025 null, Step-Back 11.9% new errors, Echterhoff framing drift.

source: Cross-study pattern (this file, c01-c26)
finding: Where reframing helped models it was a cheap, targeted rewrite (step-back, rephrase, restart with compacted Q&A, structured Dorst prompt). Where it was tested with real designers on hard open problems it did not help.
numbers: Helped: Step-Back +7 to +27 points on benchmarks; RaR about +25 points average for GPT-4; situation puzzles 2/3 -> 4/1 wins (5 puzzles). No effect: Shin 2025 N=280 across 3 LLM arms. Mixed: Echterhoff framing gap of 0.57 under one mitigation.
limits: Benchmarks with a known right answer versus open design tasks with human raters are not the same test; our own items are closer to the first.
agent_relevance: Use O8 as a gated restate or abstract step on benchmark-type items; do not expect open-ended design frame quality gains from the model alone.

source: Li et al. (2025) Situation puzzles (design of the loop)
finding: Method detail: after K=5 rounds of Q&A, keep a few confirmed items (M=3: two yes-questions and the first no-question in the example), write them into the puzzle text, and start a fresh chat session.
numbers: Best setting K=5, M=3: 22.6 questions, 2.4 guesses, 4/1. K=10, M=6: 24.2 questions, 3 guesses, 3/2.
limits: Hand-set K and M; five puzzles.
agent_relevance: A concrete, code-driven reframe trigger and compaction rule that we can copy and test on BRAINTEASER.
